common_name: Gimbornii Lawson Cypress (Dwarf Blue-Grey Globe Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, sheltered from harsh winter wind and sited where drainage is reliable.

directions: Gimbornii is a very slow-growing dwarf Lawson cypress that builds a dense, rounded to broadly conical mound of tightly congested, powdery blue-grey foliage sprays, staying far smaller and neater than the towering wild species. It is a favorite for rock gardens, conifer collections, and container plantings where its soft color and fine, compact texture read well up close. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade with shelter from drying winds, and avoid heavy or waterlogged ground, since Lawson cypress cultivars are notably prone to Phytophthora root rot when drainage is poor. Little to no pruning is needed to maintain its naturally tidy globose habit.

common_name: Minima Aurea Lawson Cypress (Dwarf Golden Conical Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun for the brightest gold color; give shelter from strong wind and ensure sharp drainage.

directions: Minima Aurea is an extremely slow-growing, dense, conical dwarf Lawson cypress with tightly packed sprays of bright golden-yellow foliage that holds its color best in full sun, fading toward yellow-green in shade. Its small stature and neat, symmetrical outline suit rock gardens, foundation plantings, and mixed dwarf conifer beds where a full-sized Lawson cypress would be unmanageable. Plant in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil and avoid heavy or poorly drained ground, which invites root rot in this genus. Because growth is so gradual, only light shaping is ever needed to keep its naturally dense, compact form.

common_name: Heatherbun Atlantic White Cedar (Dwarf Globe with Winter Plum Color)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in consistently moist to wet, acidic soil in full sun; as a selection of the native swamp-dwelling species, it tolerates poorly drained sites better than most falsecypress cultivars.

directions: Heatherbun is a compact, dense, dwarf globe selection of the native Atlantic white cedar, prized for fine, soft, blue-green summer foliage that turns a rich plum-purple in cold weather before greening up again each spring. Unlike most falsecypress, it descends from a wetland native species and is genuinely comfortable in consistently moist to seasonally wet, acidic soil, making it a useful evergreen accent for rain gardens, pond margins, and low, damp spots where many dwarf conifers would struggle. Grow in full sun for the most pronounced winter color change and densest habit, and avoid letting the site dry out completely during establishment. Its small, rounded form needs no regular pruning to stay tidy.

common_name: Verdoni Sawara Cypress (Compact Golden Threadleaf Falsecypress)

planting.note: Plant container stock in spring or fall in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest gold color; light afternoon shade helps prevent foliage scorch in the hottest climates.

directions: Verdoni is a compact, upright-conical Sawara cypress with fine, thread-like sprays of golden-yellow foliage that stay more tightly held and less mop-like than 'Golden Mop', giving it a neater, more architectural silhouette for small gardens and mixed conifer borders. Growth is slow and dense, so it needs little pruning to keep a well-furnished, symmetrical outline from the ground up. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest gold color, though a little afternoon shade helps prevent bronzing during peak summer heat. Established plants dislike soggy, poorly drained ground, which encourages root rot.

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun; a narrow, unsheared habit and slow growth rate make it a low-maintenance choice for tight spaces along foundations or walks.

directions: Holmstrup is a dense, slow-growing arborvitae that holds a naturally narrow, conical-columnar outline without shearing, its bright green foliage arranged in tidy, vertical, fan-like sprays rather than the looser sprays typical of the species. Its slim mature width makes it useful for narrow side yards, formal hedges, and tight foundation spaces where wider arborvitae cultivars would quickly crowd a path or window. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, where it holds good winter color with little of the bronzing some arborvitae show in cold weather. It is markedly slower growing than the species, so patience is needed to reach full height, but this also means less long-term pruning.

common_name: Anna's Magic Ball Arborvitae (Dwarf Golden Globe Arborvitae)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the brightest gold color; the naturally rounded form needs no shearing to stay tidy.

directions: Anna's Magic Ball is a true dwarf arborvitae that forms a dense, perfectly rounded globe of bright golden-yellow foliage without any shearing or shaping, staying compact for many years. Its small, predictable size and cheerful color make it a popular anchor for rock gardens, mixed conifer beds, and containers where a full-sized golden arborvitae would be far too large. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, which brings out the strongest gold color; foliage can green up somewhat in shadier spots. It is a low-maintenance plant that rarely needs pruning beyond removing the occasional stray shoot.

common_name: Teddy Arborvitae (Dwarf Globe with Soft Feathery Foliage)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; foliage often takes on a plum-bronze cast in cold weather and greens up again in spring.

directions: Teddy is a very dwarf, slow-growing arborvitae selected for its unusually soft, fine-textured, blue-green juvenile foliage, which stays plush and feathery rather than maturing into the coarser, scale-like sprays typical of the species. Its small, dense, rounded habit and tactile texture make it a favorite for rock gardens, troughs, and small-space plantings where visitors can appreciate it up close. Plant in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, and expect a purplish-bronze winter tone on exposed plants that fades back to blue-green as new growth emerges in spring. It needs essentially no pruning to keep its naturally tidy mounded shape.

common_name: Fire Chief Arborvitae (Dwarf Globe with Seasonal Gold-to-Red Color)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun for the strongest seasonal color shifts; the compact globe habit needs no shearing.

directions: Fire Chief is a compact, rounded dwarf arborvitae grown for its dramatic seasonal color changes, emerging bright gold-orange in spring, settling to green through summer, and flushing back to fiery orange-red in fall and winter. Its tidy globe habit and dependable size make it a strong focal point in mixed conifer beds and foundation plantings without the bulk of larger arborvitae cultivars. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun, which intensifies the color transitions; plants in more shade tend to stay greener year-round. It is slow growing and holds its rounded form with little to no pruning.

common_name: Whipcord Western Red Cedar (Weeping Threadleaf Arborvitae)

planting.note: Plant container-grown plants in spring in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; site where its cascading, cord-like texture can drape over a wall or rock without being crowded by neighbors.

directions: Whipcord is an unmistakable arborvitae cultivar whose foliage is reduced almost entirely to long, slender, cord-like strands that cascade from the branches in a shaggy, weeping mop, giving the whole plant a texture unlike any typical conifer. It forms a low, mounding to gently draping shrub rather than the upright pyramid of the species, making it a distinctive accent trailing over a wall, boulder, or raised bed edge. Grow in moist, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade, with some afternoon shade helpful in hot summer climates to keep the fine foliage from browning. Growth is slow and the plant requires no shearing, since pruning would disrupt its naturally cascading, cord-like habit.

common_name: Vilmoriniana Japanese Cedar (Very Dwarf Globe Sugi)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; extremely slow growth means little maintenance is ever needed to keep its shape.

directions: Vilmoriniana is one of the smallest and slowest-growing Japanese cedar cultivars, forming a dense, congested globe of short, tightly packed needles that advances only about an inch a year, taking decades to reach even modest size. Its foliage shifts from fresh green in summer to a deep reddish-bronze-purple through winter, adding seasonal interest to its small, sculptural form. Because of its diminutive size, it is a mainstay of rock gardens, alpine troughs, and bonsai-style plantings where a full-sized Japanese cedar would never fit. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, keeping it consistently watered through its first seasons while the compact root system establishes.

common_name: Spiralis Japanese Cedar (Granny's Ringlets Twisted-Needle Sugi)

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; the twisted needle texture is best appreciated as a specimen where it can be viewed at close range.

directions: Nicknamed Granny's Ringlets, Spiralis is an old, distinctive Japanese cedar selection whose needles curl and spiral tightly around the stems rather than lying flat, giving every branch a corkscrew, cord-like texture that is unlike any other conifer in the garden. It grows into a broadly pyramidal to irregular small tree over time, considerably more slowly and often more compact than the wild species, while still developing real tree-like stature given decades to mature. Site it as a textural specimen in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil, where its unusual curled foliage catches the light and reads as a conversation piece year-round. It needs little routine pruning beyond removing dead interior growth.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; some protection from intense midday sun helps keep the cream-gold new growth from scorching.

directions: Sekkan-sugi is a variegated Japanese cedar selection whose new spring growth emerges a striking creamy yellow-gold, gradually softening to pale green by summer and creating a two-toned, luminous effect across the canopy through the growing season. It forms a broadly pyramidal small to medium tree, slower and more restrained than the straight species, and works well as a bright focal specimen against darker evergreens where its glowing new growth stands out. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade, since intense full sun can scorch the pale new foliage, while too much shade mutes the gold coloring. Established plants need little care beyond removing any reverted all-green shoots to preserve the variegation.

common_name: Compressa Japanese Cedar (Miniature Dense Globe Sugi)

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; its miniature, congested habit suits close viewing in troughs and rock gardens.

directions: Compressa is a true miniature Japanese cedar, forming an exceptionally dense, tightly congested globe of short, fine needles that stays smaller and slower-growing than even other dwarf sugi cultivars like 'Globosa Nana'. Foliage is blue-green through the growing season and takes on a bronze-purple tinge in winter cold, adding subtle seasonal interest to its small, sculptural form. Its diminutive size makes it a natural fit for alpine troughs, rock gardens, and miniature conifer collections where full-sized Japanese cedar selections would be entirely out of scale. Grow in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade, and expect it to hold its neat globose shape for many years without any pruning.
